Elizabeth: you okay? you went silent after the meeting
Salma: he did it again. called my forecast "kindergarten work" in front of eleven people
Salma: two of them looked at their laps. nobody said anything
Elizabeth: I'm so sorry. That's not okay
Salma: I keep wondering if I really am that bad at this. my hands were shaking
Elizabeth: One weak forecast doesn't make it fair to belittle you in front of a room. You can be corrected without being humiliated
Salma: I typed the date and his exact words into my phone right after
Elizabeth: Good. Keep doing that. Would you talk to Ravi? He's been here ten years and people trust him. Then HR if it continues
Salma: Ravi first. Then HR
Elizabeth: I'll sit next to you in the next meeting. Walk at lunch?
Salma: yes. thanks for not saying it's just his style

qa.q: How many people were in the room when Salma's forecast was called kindergarten work?
qa.a: Eleven people were in the room.

qa.q: Why were Salma's hands shaking, and what doubt was Salma carrying?
qa.a: Salma was humiliated and shaken, and doubted being any good at the job.

qa.q: What has Salma done to keep a record, and what is planned next?
qa.a: Salma saved the date and the manager's exact words in a phone note, and plans to talk to Ravi first, then HR if it continues.

qa.q: Why might the two colleagues who looked at their laps have said nothing?
qa.a: They may have felt uncomfortable or worried about drawing the manager's attention, though the chat does not say.

grounding: A manager belittles a worker in a meeting; the worker feels humiliated, documents it, and turns to a trusted senior and HR.

passage:
First Tuesday. In the weekly review, Lavanya, the sales head, held up Yogesh's report in front of twelve people. "Did a child write this? Honestly, Yogesh, I expect more from a peon." A few people laughed nervously. Yogesh stared at the table, face burning. That night he couldn't eat. He kept thinking he must be stupid.

The next Monday. It happened again, this time to Meena from accounts. Yogesh watched her eyes fill. Something shifted in him. It wasn't him. It was how Lavanya treated people. He opened a notebook and started writing: dates, exact words, who was present. He asked Meena if she'd do the same.

Three weeks later. With six dated entries and Meena's notes, Yogesh met Mr. Chauhan, a senior director he trusted, and then HR. HR opened a formal review. Yogesh also started walking in the evenings again, and told his sister everything. He was still nervous in meetings. But he no longer believed he deserved it.

qa.q: How many people were in the weekly review when Lavanya mocked Yogesh's report?
What was Yogesh feeling on the first Tuesday night?
qa.a: Yogesh felt humiliated and ashamed, unable to eat and believing he must be stupid.

qa.q: What steps did Yogesh take to protect himself?
qa.a: He recorded dated incidents with exact words and witnesses, went to a trusted senior and HR, and looked after his health and support.

qa.q: How did Meena seem to experience Lavanya's comments?
qa.a: Meena was hurt and humiliated, her eyes filling with tears in front of everyone.

grounding: The story shows a young man belittled by his manager in meetings who feels humiliated, realises it is not his fault, documents incidents, seeks HR and senior support and protects his health.

passage:
Pradeep, you say your boss mocks you in meetings and you think it's because you're weak. Listen to your Nitin mama.

At twenty-four I worked at a textile firm under a man called Grover. Every Monday he picked someone to tear apart. Often me. "Nitin, your brain is on holiday." "Nitin, go and sell peanuts instead." People laughed so they wouldn't be next. I started getting headaches every Sunday night. I was sure it was my fault.

Then one day I saw him do it to Mrs. Fernandes, who had worked there twenty years and was brilliant. That was my turning point. It wasn't about us. It was him.

I began writing it down in a small diary: date, words, who heard. After two months I took it to Mr. Kulkarni, the senior partner, whom everyone respected. He read it silently, then said, "This stops."

Grover was moved within the year. The headaches stopped sooner, the day I stopped believing him.

qa.q: What did Grover tell Nitin to go and sell?
qa.a: He told him to go and sell peanuts.

qa.q: How did young Nitin feel about Grover's mockery at first?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and anxious, getting headaches every Sunday and believing it was his fault.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nitin's story?
qa.a: Seeing Grover humiliate the brilliant Mrs. Fernandes showed him it wasn't his fault, so he documented incidents and went to a respected senior partner.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Fernandes have felt when Grover mocked her?
qa.a: She was likely humiliated and hurt, even after twenty years of excellent work.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young man belittled by his manager who realised it was not his fault, documented incidents and sought help from a trusted senior.
